en: CLAUDE : Sir, I am grateful to you for understanding that it is indeed completely impossible. I cannot fathom how such an idea could even have crossed my daughter's mind.
OSMONDE (to Mégal) : Think it over.
MÉGAL : Mademoiselle, I feel that... I have no right to accept.
OSMONDE : Why no right?
MÉGAL : It would be abusing the very affection you have shown my children. I would feel I were committing a wrongful act.
OSMONDE : Toward my parents?
MÉGAL (deeply troubled) : Not only toward your parents.
CLAUDE (holding out his hand to him) : Sir, you are an honorable man, but you will agree with me that there is no reason to prolong this conversation. When I have set my reasons before my daughter...
OSMONDE : I know them.
CLAUDE : You can see that my daughter is not in her normal state at this moment.
MÉGAL (to Claude) : I cannot tell you how much I would have liked to accept such a generous offer... it is more than regret. (His voice breaks.) It is a kind of heartbreak... I...

OSMONDE (to Claude) : It is extremely simple. If you do not leave me free to act as I please, I will go and sit at the bedside... of the sick man we were speaking of earlier, and I shall not leave him until the end. (To Mégal.) It concerns a relative to whom I shall devote myself, if you refuse my offer.
CLAUDE (to Mégal) : Sir, I beg of you to leave me alone with her. No one can know what I am suffering.
OSMONDE (to Mégal) : See you shortly.
MÉGAL (to Claude, with a sort of commiseration) : Sir, from the bottom of my heart, I... (He shakes his hand and exits.)
[SCENE IX]
OSMONDE : Choose.
CLAUDE : I do not have to choose. You are staying here.
OSMONDE : Under no circumstances will I stay here.
CLAUDE : Take care.
OSMONDE : Try as I might, your threats...
CLAUDE : But who on earth are you?
OSMONDE : I am not your daughter... Come, remember that deep down you never gain much by holding people against their will.
CLAUDE : If it is your mother you are speaking of, there was a day when she begged me not to drive her away.
OSMONDE : Then what do you blame yourself for?
CLAUDE : The next day she was begging me to grant her freedom. (Osmonde gives a slight, scornful shrug of her shoulders.)
OSMONDE : As for me, I know perfectly well what I want.
CLAUDE : I will not let you throw yourself into that man's arms.
OSMONDE : You cannot prevent anything.
CLAUDE : Your grandmother will take you to Switzerland.
OSMONDE : Come now, let us be reasonable.
CLAUDE : Your mother did not possess this monstrous composure.

OSMONDE : Pity for her, and probably for everyone here. Here is a young, vigorous man, chained to a madwoman... He loves me, and I love him too. Between him and me there is only a convention, a lie, by which neither of us is fooled. If out of pure cowardice I shrink back, it is not hard to guess what degrading consolations he will fall back on.
CLAUDE : You cherish no illusions...
OSMONDE : No illusions whatsoever; if I can save him from that shame...
CLAUDE : You are nothing but a corrupted child.
OSMONDE : I see that your principles are holding firm—that is fortunate indeed.
CLAUDE : It is as though your conscience were abolished...
OSMONDE : Conscience... you must admit that its oracles are highly questionable. Perhaps I am mistaken, but your own example...
CLAUDE : So that is the lesson you draw from my life.
OSMONDE : For my part, I think the essential thing is not to let oneself be fooled... I mean...
CLAUDE : And you imagine you are not deluding yourself when you claim that it is out of charity, out of goodness of soul, that you give yourself to this man?

OSMONDE : I said no such thing... It is all too clear that if he were not attractive to me... I am simply pointing out that even if one believes in virtue, in love of one's neighbor, in the whole business, as Fred calls it, well then! my decision is still very well justified. Take it from that angle if the other burns your fingers. After all, I am going to build a sort of home myself; of course, you won't be invited to bless it, but all in all... My poor father, you remind me of those people at the pension in Évilard who would go every morning to look at the Alps through the stained glass panes of the veranda... seen that way, the landscape seemed so much more beautiful to them, but at the same time, they regretted that it wasn't a natural effect; they argued endlessly about it, never managing to agree with themselves. You are like them: you don't know what you prefer, and you make yourself wretched. The great difference between us, you see, is that I can no longer take any of that seriously. Perhaps it is because I have heard too much pontificating around me about our duties, about our debt to God. When you've heard about your soul every Sunday from ten to eleven, not to mention daily prayers... There are certain words, certain ideas... I don't know, it seems to me one ought to feel a kind of shudder, a kind of vertigo every time they are uttered before you. Well, no! Your Sunday sermon is rather like the household accounts. I believe that if it weren't a sort of routine even for you, if I had had someone near me who lived in terror or in dazzling wonder... But a religion like yours, after all, changes nothing at all. It is a backdrop, nothing more. Besides, the Good Samaritan over there resembles you to an unbelievable degree!... Don't look at me with that miserable expression, father; that is blackmail, it isn't worthy of you.
CLAUDE : If you leave, I will have nothing left.

OSMONDE : But it would be worse if I stayed. Life for the three of us now... after what we have said to one another... To be able to live together, people must keep at least a minimum of illusions about each other. And besides, consider what a fine task I shall have to fulfill: replacing the mother who will never return. Come now! Think of that. The colored panes have their good points, after all. One shouldn't be ashamed to use them. (A silence.)
[SCENE X]
THE SAME, EDMÉE
EDMÉE (she appears unsteady) : Who was here just now?
OSMONDE : Monsieur Mégal came for a moment.
EDMÉE : Who gave him permission to come here?
OSMONDE : I had to speak with him in Father's presence.
EDMÉE (to Claude) : So you were here?
CLAUDE : Yes.
EDMÉE : What does all this mean?
OSMONDE : A decision was made in your absence. I am quite ready to inform you of it, but I warn you that I refuse to let it be questioned.
EDMÉE : You refuse?
OSMONDE : Absolutely. Monsieur Mégal is willing to have me as governess for his children.
CLAUDE (under his breath) : That is not even true.
OSMONDE : I'll take it upon myself to convert him.
EDMÉE (to Claude) : You are letting her do this? So that is your authority over her...
CLAUDE (with sudden violence) : I have no authority over Monsieur Sandier's daughter. I merely observe that she is worthy of her mother and is following her example.
EDMÉE : Claude!

CLAUDE : Now listen to me, Edmée: this is probably the last time I shall have the occasion to make my thinking known to you; for I have no desire to dispute you any longer with the interesting victim over whom you have been growing so tender these past few days.
EDMÉE : What? You are casting me out?
CLAUDE : I would feel scruples about depriving that dying man any longer of the tender care you are burning to lavish upon him.
OSMONDE : Father, you have that same look on your face again from earlier; you are not master of yourself.
CLAUDE (brutally) : What are you doing here? Why don't you go come to terms with that fellow regarding your conditions?
OSMONDE : Conditions?
CLAUDE : Unless you believe he expects to take you in au pair?
OSMONDE (with insulting sweetness) : It doesn't matter; I bear you no ill will. (She exits.)
[SCENE XI]
EDMÉE : Claude, stop her!
CLAUDE : It is up to you to use your influence.
EDMÉE : Stop her.
CLAUDE : From this day forward, I take no further interest in your daughter or in yourself.
EDMÉE : You are cruel!
CLAUDE : One of the few reproaches you had not yet leveled against me.
EDMÉE : Remember that you forgave me.
CLAUDE : She said that in all seriousness... Then you do not realize that the very word 'forgiveness' now... Oh! No, enough. These explanations turn my stomach.
EDMÉE : Mine too, I assure you.

CLAUDE : What I told you earlier was entirely sincere. Now that she is leaving us, there is no reason for us to go on living together. You have, it seems, great duties toward someone else. You will be able to fulfill them in good conscience from now on. As for me, it is likely that I shall resign the ministry.
EDMÉE (with sudden dread) : That cannot be true.
CLAUDE : What little strength I believed I still possessed, I feel I have lost.
EDMÉE : Faith cannot fail you like that all at once—it isn't possible.
CLAUDE : I do not know; perhaps genuine faith was never given to me.
EDMÉE : Genuine faith... yet remember, when we were betrothed, the way you spoke of life, the tone in which you uttered certain words... you were sincere.
CLAUDE : I was sincere; I was happy.

EDMÉE : Your eyes shone; it seems to me sometimes that it was because of that look that I married you... Around me, no one spoke as you did, and they all had dull faces. But you, when you spoke those words, merely by the accent with which you pronounced them... it was like a world you opened before me.
CLAUDE : And the girl confessed to me not ten minutes ago that those very same phrases, repeated too often, had driven her away from faith.
EDMÉE : They were not the same; they were new then, they were intact.
CLAUDE : I opened a world to you? What kind of world was it?
EDMÉE : I do not know.

CLAUDE : Remember what followed. The first months of our marriage. Those doubts that besieged me. The long walks you took all alone, returning tired, sullen, your face closed off. To everything I said, you answered only in monosyllables, and I resented you for it.
EDMÉE : You never told me.

CLAUDE : Did I love you back then? And you, did you love me? We do not remember; perhaps we never even knew. (A silence.) It was on the faith of a glance or an intonation that you pledged your life. A glance that promised... what? That mysterious promise was never kept, and that is the whole history of our life together... And when I think of God, it is the same. I believed at times that He was speaking to me, and perhaps it was only a deceitful exaltation. Who am I? When I try to grasp myself, I elude my own grasp. A moment ago I thought I hated you; it seemed I wanted to bruise you, to cast you out, to trample you... And now it has passed... He is fortunate, don't you think?
EDMÉE : Of whom are you speaking?
CLAUDE : Of... him.
EDMÉE : Why is he fortunate, Claude?
CLAUDE : Because he will soon be done.
EDMÉE : Death does not frighten you?
CLAUDE : No, I don't think so... It is still man's only chance, after all. Even if it is not a door that opens.
EDMÉE : You are braver than I.
CLAUDE : Are you afraid of being judged?
EDMÉE : Yes... I don't know...
CLAUDE : And I, on the contrary... To be known as one is... or else to sleep.
EDMÉE : Why are you smiling? What are you thinking of?

CLAUDE : Do you remember above Saint-Loup, that place where the ground drops away sharply... There is a great green cleft at the bottom of which the Ravenouze flows. When the weather is clear, you can see the Trois Becs at the far end of the valley. We could go there one evening after dinner, as we did in the very earliest days, and then...
EDMÉE (in terror) : No, no, I don't want to...
FÉLICIE (offstage) : But no, Mademoiselle, I will inform the Pastor. (She enters.)
CLAUDE : What is it, Félicie?
FÉLICIE : It is Mademoiselle Aubonneau with little René, so she told me.
CLAUDE : Why did you say I was in?
FÉLICIE : Well, aren't you here? (Claude and Edmée look at each other.) Won't you come in, Mademoiselle?
[SCENE XII]
THE SAME, MLLE AUBONNEAU, LITTLE RENÉ
MLLE AUBONNEAU : Good day, Madame; good day, Pastor. I do apologize for coming at such an hour, but it is René's day out, and we have been running errands all afternoon.
CLAUDE : Not at all, it is very kind of you.
MLLE AUBONNEAU : We were all the more eager to come today because it is your wedding anniversary.
EDMÉE : The twenty-first of December, that is true... it is true.
MLLE AUBONNEAU (to René) : Well now, you might give your bouquet to Madame Lemoyne. How anyone can be so clumsy! (René gives the bouquet to Edmée.)
EDMÉE : That is far too kind.
CLAUDE : Yes, it is truly...
MLLE AUBONNEAU : It is the least we could do, when I think of all we owe you... His mother (she points to René) asked me to give you her best regards.
CLAUDE : How is she?
MLLE AUBONNEAU : She's so-so, as usual, but she doesn't complain; and besides, as she says: 'Without Pastor and Madame Lemoyne, the Good Lord only knows where I would be.'
EDMÉE : What?
MLLE AUBONNEAU : Why! Don't you remember that you are the ones who got her admitted to the Rue Michel-Bizot?
CLAUDE : It is true, she is there now.
MLLE AUBONNEAU : With the deaconesses of the Rue Michel-Bizot. As she says: 'Everyone is so kind to me.'
CLAUDE : So much the better.

MLLE AUBONNEAU : And she specifically asked me to tell you that she prays often for you, Pastor, though you surely have little need of her prayers, and also for Madame Lemoyne, and for Mademoiselle Osmonde.
CLAUDE : Thank you, thank you.
MLLE AUBONNEAU : As we always say, pastors like you are few and far between.
LITTLE RENÉ : Could I wish my godmother a Happy New Year?
MLLE AUBONNEAU : Because he will be going to my mother's, in Charente, for New Year's.
EDMÉE : That is true; I was forgetting that Osmonde is his godmother... (She goes to the back and calls out: Osmonde! Osmonde!)
OSMONDE (offstage) : What is it?
EDMÉE : Your godson is here; he would like to say hello to you... Little René Aubonneau...
MLLE AUBONNEAU : No, his name is Ferrandon, after my brother-in-law.
EDMÉE : Quite right, I beg your pardon. Little Ferrandon, Osmonde.
OSMONDE (from outside) : I'm in the middle of packing.
MLLE AUBONNEAU : Mademoiselle Osmonde is going on a journey?
EDMÉE : She is preparing to take up a position.
MLLE AUBONNEAU : She has always been so serious! And of course it is a position... something quite...
CLAUDE : A post as governess...
MLLE AUBONNEAU : Really? And I suppose it is with people you know...
CLAUDE : It is with a gentleman whose wife has lost her mind.
MLLE AUBONNEAU : How dreadful! The things one sees nowadays...
CLAUDE : There are two little girls there...
MLLE AUBONNEAU : And of course the gentleman is already of a certain age. I am sure she will be a true mother to those little darlings.
OSMONDE (half-opening the door) : Here, René, if you'd like to come in. Good day, Mademoiselle, please do come in for a moment too.
MLLE AUBONNEAU : I am so glad to see you.
RENÉ (entering) : Godmother, I wish you a very Happy New Year. (Claude and Edmée remain alone.)
EDMÉE : There... that is whom we shall have to live for, now.
CLAUDE (lost in his thoughts) : To be known as one is...
